segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since we have these promises, then, dear friends, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Make room for us. We wronged no one, we corrupted no one, we took advantage of no one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I do not say this to condemn you, for I have said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Great is my frankness toward you; great is my boasting about you. I am filled with comfort; I am overflowing with joy in all our affliction.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no relief; we were afflicted in every way—conflicts outside, fears within.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and not only by his arrival but also by the comfort with which he was comforted over you, as he reported to us your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even if I grieved you with my letter, I do not regret it. Even if I did regret it (I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while),

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: now I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into turning back. For you were grieved in God's way, so that you might suffer no loss through us in anything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For grief in God's way brings about a turning back that leads to salvation and leaves no regret, but the world's grief produces death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For see what earnestness this very thing, being grieved in God's way, has produced in you—and what a defense of yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment of the wrong! In every way you have shown yourselves to be innocent in the matter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, even though I wrote to you, it was not on account of the one who did the wrong, nor on account of the one who was wronged, but so that your earnestness for us might be made plain to you before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Because of this we have been comforted. And on top of our comfort, we rejoiced even more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I have boasted to him about you in anything, I was not put to shame; but just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And his affection for you is all the greater as he remembers the obedience of all of you, how you received him with fear and trembling.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I rejoice that in everything I have confidence in you.

notes.note: The verb means to make space or have room for something. Paul is resuming the appeal of 6:11-13, where he said his heart was wide open to the Corinthians and asked them to open wide in return. Many translations add 'in your hearts' to make the link explicit.

The Greek word covers both outspokenness and confidence. Some translations take it here as 'I have great confidence in you', which pairs well with the boasting that follows. The sense of open, unguarded speech is the more common one in the period and fits Paul's defence of his blunt earlier letter.

notes.traditional: comforteth those that are cast down
notes.note: The wording echoes the Greek version of Isaiah 49:13, where God is said to have comforted the lowly of his people. The word can mean 'humble' or 'lowly' in status; here the context of exhaustion and fear points to people brought low in spirit.

This is the word used elsewhere for the 'coming' of Christ. Its ordinary meaning is simply someone's arrival and resulting presence, and that is the sense here. Paul had been waiting anxiously for Titus to return from Corinth with news (2:12-13).

This is the letter Paul says in 2:3-4 he wrote 'with many tears' after a painful episode at Corinth. Most scholars think it is lost. A minority identify it with 1 Corinthians or with chapters 10-13 of this letter.

The sentence is grammatically rough in Greek, and the manuscripts differ. Some add 'for' after 'I see', and a few read 'seeing'. The translation follows the shorter reading and treats the clause as a parenthesis. The overall sense is the same in each form.

'Repentance' in modern English suggests chiefly feeling sorry. Paul here distinguishes the grief from what it leads to, a change of direction toward God like the prophets' call to 'return'. Most translations keep 'repentance' as an established term understood to include a change of life.

notes.traditional: after a godly manner; godly sorrow
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'according to God', repeated in verses 10 and 11. It means grief of the kind God approves or intends, as opposed to 'the world's grief'. The traditional 'godly sorrow' conveys much the same idea. Some translations render it 'as God intended'.

The adjective 'unregretted' could describe either the turning back or the salvation; the Greek grammar allows both. The translation leaves it attached to the whole outcome. The word picks up Paul's 'I do not regret it' in verse 8. It is a different Greek word from the one rendered 'turning back'.

The word means the carrying out of justice. It can refer to punishing an offender or to vindicating the injured party. Here it most likely refers to the congregation's disciplining of the offender (compare 2:6), though 'readiness to see justice done' is also a fair rendering.

notes.phrase: the one who did the wrong
notes.traditional: his cause that had done the wrong
notes.note: Paul does not name either party, and their identity is uncertain. The offender is usually linked with the person disciplined in 2:5-11, and many scholars think the one wronged was Paul himself or one of his associates. An older view connects the case with the man of 1 Corinthians 5.

candidates.reason: It ranges across comfort, encouragement, appeal and exhortation throughout Paul and Acts, and translations vary widely even within one passage.
It is rendered affliction, tribulation, trouble, distress or suffering across books, obscuring a recurring New Testament theme.
It shifts between open speech, boldness and confidence in John, Acts, Paul and Hebrews, and needs sense-by-sense defaults.
Literally the inward parts, it is variously rendered heart, affection, compassion or bowels, and the related verb is important in the Gospels.
It is frequent in Paul with both positive and negative force, and translations alternate between boast, pride, glory and exult.
